passage:
Monday: Rukmini's period started, and Paati told her to sit apart on the back verandah and stay out of the kitchen and the puja room. Rukmini ate from a separate plate, cramps twisting her stomach, feeling as if she'd done something dirty. When her brother Akash asked loudly why she was sitting outside, she wanted to disappear.
Wednesday: Amma sat with her on the verandah with a hot-water bottle and a mat. 'Paati's customs come from her own mother,' Amma said. 'We'll respect the puja room. But you'll sleep in your own bed, eat with us, and you have nothing to be ashamed of.' She answered all Rukmini's questions plainly.
Next month: Rukmini told Akash calmly, 'It's my period. It's normal.' He shrugged and passed her the chutney.

qa.q: What did Amma bring to the verandah?
qa.a: A hot-water bottle and a mat.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel on Monday eating from a separate plate?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, as if she had done something dirty, and wanted to disappear when Akash asked loudly.

qa.q: How did Amma balance Paati's customs with Rukmini's dignity?
qa.a: She kept the puja-room custom but made sure Rukmini slept in her own bed, ate with the family, had comfort and got plain answers.

qa.q: How might Akash see periods by the next month?
qa.a: Akash saw it as ordinary once Rukmini explained calmly, simply shrugging and passing the chutney.

grounding: A girl told to hide her period learns shame, and her mother respects family custom while ensuring comfort, information and dignity.

passage: On the morning of her chemistry practical, Dolma woke doubled over with period cramps worse than ever. The school in Gangtok was a steep twenty-minute climb, and the practical could not easily be moved. She went anyway, pale and sweating, and nearly fainted over the burette. When her lab partner Aditi called the teacher, Dolma begged, 'Don't make a fuss, they'll say I'm dramatic.' The teacher didn't make a fuss. She had Dolma lie down in the sick room, called her mother and arranged for the practical to be taken the following week. That evening Dolma's mother said, 'Pain that stops you standing isn't something to just bear,' and booked a doctor's appointment.

qa.q: What did Dolma nearly faint over?
qa.a: The burette.

qa.q: What was Dolma worried about when she begged them not to make a fuss?
qa.a: She was anxious that people would call her dramatic for her pain.

qa.q: What did the adults do that was right?
qa.a: The teacher believed her, let her lie down, called her mother and moved the practical, and her mother booked a doctor for the severe pain.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt seeing Dolma nearly faint?
qa.a: Aditi was probably frightened and concerned, which is why Aditi called the teacher despite Dolma's pleading.

grounding: A student with painful periods fears being called dramatic, and being believed and taken to a doctor prevents needless suffering.

passage: In the university biology lab, Deepika kept a small notebook next to her pipettes. Kiran, her lab partner, finally asked what she was always jotting down. 'My cycle and my moods,' Deepika said, unembarrassed. 'Three months of notes. See? Around these days I'm tired and tear up at nothing. Around these, I'm sharp and can manage long runs.' She had moved the fiddly cell counts to her strong week and kept the low days for reading papers and leaving on time. 'I used to think I was just weak on those days,' she said. 'Now it's just planning.' Kiran looked at the neat columns. 'That's smarter than my to-do list.'

qa.q: What does Deepika keep next to her pipettes?
qa.a: A small notebook.

qa.q: How did Deepika use to feel about her low days?
qa.a: She used to feel inadequate, thinking she was just weak on those days.

qa.q: How does Deepika use her notes?
qa.a: She plans the fiddly cell counts for her strong week and keeps low days for reading papers and leaving on time.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Deepika's notebook?
qa.a: Kiran is impressed, finding the neat columns smarter than a to-do list.

grounding: A young woman who tracks her cycle plans rest and lighter work for low days without treating them as weakness.

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Parul slammed the laptop shut and pushed away her plate. Their flatmate Rohan laughed from the sofa. 'Must be that time of the month.' Lavanya saw Parul's jaw tighten. 'Rohan, don't,' Lavanya said, and sat down next to Parul. 'What's going on? You seem really upset.' Parul breathed out. 'My manager gave my project to someone else. After I did all the groundwork.' 'That's genuinely unfair,' Lavanya said. 'No wonder you're angry.' Rohan went quiet, then muttered sorry. Later Parul told Lavanya, 'If you'd blamed hormones too, I'd never have told you.'

qa.q: What did Parul's manager do?
qa.a: Gave Parul's project to someone else.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when Rohan made the 'time of the month' joke?
qa.a: She felt dismissed and even angrier, her jaw tightening.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya's question work better than Rohan's joke?
qa.a: Asking what was going on let Parul share the real problem, an unfair decision at work, instead of shutting her down.

qa.q: How might Rohan feel once he heard the real reason?
qa.a: Rohan probably felt embarrassed and sorry, realising his joke had dismissed a real problem.

grounding: A friend asks how a young woman is feeling instead of blaming her mood on her cycle, which keeps honest talk open.

passage: In the hospital's billing department, Deepak noticed that Tenzin had been quiet all morning, one hand pressed low on her stomach, her face pale under the tube light. She kept working through the queue of files without a break. At lunch, two colleagues in the corridor joked, 'Tenzin's in a mood again, stay away.' Deepak felt uncomfortable and said, 'Leave it, yaar.' He didn't ask her anything personal. He just put a cup of hot tea on her desk and said, 'I'll cover the counter for an hour if you want to rest in the staff room.' Tenzin looked up, relieved. 'Thanks. Bad cramps today.' 'No explanation needed,' Deepak said, and took her seat.

qa.q: What did Deepak put on Tenzin's desk?
qa.a: A cup of hot tea.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when colleagues joked about Tenzin's mood?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable with the joke and wanted it stopped.

qa.q: What made Deepak's help respectful?
qa.a: He offered practical cover and rest without personal questions or jokes, keeping her privacy.

qa.q: What was it like for Tenzin to be offered cover?
qa.a: She felt relieved and grateful, able to rest without having to explain herself.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate quietly struggling with cramps and offers a break and privacy instead of jokes.

subtopic: Menstrual cycle effects on mood and coping
passage: Every month, in the week before her period, Sarika's life in their Kochi flat seemed to fall apart. She cried through meetings, snapped at Joseph over nothing, and one month called in sick three days running because she couldn't face anyone. Her mother said, 'All women go through it. Bear it.' Sarika had borne it for years. One evening, after a week of barely sleeping, she told Joseph, 'It feels like I disappear for a week and a stranger lives here.' Joseph held her hand. 'This isn't something you just tolerate. Let's see a doctor.' He found a women's health clinic, went with her, and helped her write down her monthly notes. The doctor took her seriously and made a plan with her.

qa.q: What did Sarika's mother say?
qa.a: 'All women go through it. Bear it.'

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she said a stranger lives there?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and lost, as if she disappeared for a week every month.

qa.q: What steps did Joseph take?
qa.a: He refused to treat it as something to tolerate, found a clinic, went with her and helped write down her monthly notes.

qa.q: How might Joseph have experienced the snapping over nothing?
qa.a: Joseph may have felt hurt at times, yet he saw a real problem rather than a character flaw.

grounding: Overwhelming monthly distress that disrupts work and relationships is taken seriously and brought to a doctor.

subtype: Partner unsure how to help during pregnancy [Receiver]
passage: In their village near Thanjavur, Karthik felt like a spare part. Since Selvi's pregnancy began, her mother and aunts filled the house with advice, and Selvi was tired and sick every morning. When he offered suggestions from a video about food, she snapped, 'Everyone's telling me what to do!' He went out to the paddy field feeling useless and shut out, anxious too, though still excited about the baby. His uncle, watching him kick at the bund, said, 'Stop advising. Listen. Wash the vessels. Go with her to the clinic.' The next week Karthik swept the house before dawn, sat with Selvi through her worries without fixing them, and held the file at the health centre appointment. On the bus home she leaned on his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Karthik hold at the health centre appointment?
qa.a: The file.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel in the paddy field?
qa.a: He felt useless, shut out and anxious, even while excited about the baby.

qa.q: What helped Karthik grow closer to Selvi?
qa.a: Listening instead of advising, sharing chores like sweeping, and going to the appointment with her.

qa.q: How might Selvi have experienced Karthik's video advice?
qa.a: She probably felt overwhelmed and pressured, already tired and surrounded by everyone's instructions.

grounding: A young husband feels excited, anxious and left out during pregnancy and finds that listening, chores and appointments build closeness.

passage: In her Aizawl flat, Lalremsiami was folding tiny baby socks when she suddenly started crying. Ten minutes earlier she had been laughing at the baby's kicks, a hand on her belly. Now she was thinking about the stairs, her job, whether she'd know what to do, and she was so tired she could barely lift her arms. Her friend Nandini, visiting with a pineapple, sat beside her. 'Happy and scared in the same hour. Is that terrible?' Lalremsiami asked. 'No,' Nandini said. 'It's a big thing. It's allowed to feel big.' She didn't tell her to cheer up. She just folded the rest of the socks with her, and Lalremsiami laughed again at how small they were.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami folding?
qa.a: Tiny baby socks.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Lalremsiami have within an hour?
qa.a: She felt joyful at the kicks, then scared and tearful about the future, and very tired.

qa.q: Why was Nandini's response helpful?
qa.a: Nandini accepted the mixed feelings instead of correcting them or saying cheer up, and simply stayed and helped.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt seeing Lalremsiami cry?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt tender and protective, choosing calm company over advice.

grounding: A pregnant woman feels joy, fear, tears and fatigue in one hour, and a friend accepts the mix rather than correcting it.

passage: Liam painted the spare room in their Dublin flat a pale yellow and told everyone he was buzzing about the baby. It was true. But at night he lay awake doing sums: rent, childcare, his contract ending in March. He already missed Saturday football with his mates, and felt guilty for missing it. He kept quiet, thinking Elif had enough to carry. Instead he went silent at dinner and worked late. One night Elif said, 'You've disappeared on me. What's going on?' He almost said 'nothing'. Then it all came out. Elif listened, then laughed softly. 'I'm scared about money too. Let's be scared together, and make a plan.'

qa.q: What colour did Liam paint the spare room?
qa.a: Pale yellow.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling at night?
qa.a: He felt anxious about money and his contract, and guilty for missing his freedom, while still excited about the baby.

qa.q: What changed when Liam shared his worries?
qa.a: Elif shared her own fears, and they could plan together instead of Liam withdrawing.

qa.q: How had Elif experienced Liam's silence?
qa.a: Elif felt he had disappeared on her, left alone and worried by the silence and late nights.

grounding: An expectant father hides worries about money and freedom until sharing them with his partner turns withdrawal into support.

passage: Five days after the baby came home to their Pune flat, Mehak cried because the dal was too salty. Then she cried because the baby looked so perfect. At three in the morning she cried because she couldn't remember when she'd last slept. 'I'm meant to be happy. What's wrong with me?' she sobbed to her sister Reena, who had come to stay. Reena took the baby. 'Nothing's wrong with you. Your body's been through a storm and you haven't slept. Eat this, then sleep. I'll wake you for the feed.' Reena cooked, did the laundry and fielded visitors. Slowly Mehak laughed more. 'And if the heaviness doesn't lift, or it worries you, we tell the doctor,' Reena said. Mehak nodded.

qa.q: Why did Mehak cry about the dal?
qa.a: It was too salty.

qa.q: What was Mehak worried about when she sobbed to Reena?
qa.a: She was worried something was wrong with her because she felt tearful and overwhelmed instead of simply happy.

qa.q: What practical help did Reena give?
qa.a: She took the baby so Mehak could eat and sleep, cooked, did laundry and handled visitors, and agreed they'd tell the doctor if it didn't lift.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt seeing her sister cry at three in the morning?
qa.a: Reena probably felt tender and protective, wanting to take the load so Mehak could rest.

grounding: A new mother cries easily and feels overwhelmed in the first days after birth, and rest, food, reassurance and help ease it.
